reference: Walter W. Skeat, Malay Magic (1900), pp.85–96: greater gods, sea-spirit family and black/white genii
review: Read pp.85–96. Recorded all named members of the sea-spirit and Black/White Genie family passages. Kept reported identities, author conjectures, and biological versus material origin distinct; unnamed wives and seven children remain unnamed.

reference: Roland B. Dixon, Oceanic Mythology (1916), pp.160–163, 173: Toba, Dairi and Karo accounts
review: Read the three separately labelled creation accounts and Dairi creation of humankind. Named Mula Dyadi resolved to existing record; unnamed sons, brides, birds and human pair remain contextual entities rather than conjectural named targets.

reference: Andi’ Zainal Abidin, The Emergence of Early Kingdoms in South Sulawesi (1983), pp.456, 460–461 and 465, sections IV.2 and V.2
review: Read section IV.2 and contextual distinction between epic and historical kings. Corrected generation error, preserved direct versus grandparent descent, and supplied named spouse/other-parent records. This passage calls We Nyili’timo a niece whereas other summaries call her a cousin; do not force a biological cousin edge.

reference: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java, second edition (1830), vol.I pp.418–428: synopsis of the Kanda
review: Read the Kanda synopsis pp.418–428. All named direct kin through the narrated Brama/Chitra Bahar/Rahwana branch are registered, with creation and adoption separated. Watu Gunung’s independent episode, later Rama incarnations and unnamed intermediates are separately inventoried for further identity review; Indra/Sakra reserved to their owner.

reference: Batara Guru, Javanese portrayal and names
review: Read the Javanese section for the Shiva identification and Manikmaya/Girinata names. Its unsourced Bugis concubine list is not treated as validated genealogy.

reference: Martin Gaenszle, Redefining Kiranti Religion in Contemporary Nepal (2016), author preprint pp.7–8, section 2
review: Read section 2. Supports modern identification, sisters and pilgrimage context; does not establish their parents. Distinguish local oral traditions from a homogenized pantheon.

reference: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1830), vol.II Appendix H, chapters I–III, pp.cxii–cxix: Manek Maya
review: Read chapters I–III through p.cxix. Preserved cosmic origin, motherless generation, alternate Kanekaputra descent and incompatible Durga–Kala relationships. Places, substances and weapons are not person IDs.

reference: Shiva Purana 3.18.24–31, eleven Rudras born to Surabhi and Kashyapa
review: Read 24–31. Eleven distinct named manifestations; names shared with other figures do not select those identities. Kaśyapa endpoint belongs to the Sakra lane. No unnamed millions of followers fabricated.

reference: Shiva Purana 3.13.1–8, Vishvanara and Shucishmati; 3.14 birth narrative
review: Read 1–8 and the household’s request for a son. Kāla is context-qualified; Śāṇḍilya lineage does not specify a direct biological father.

reference: Shiva Purana 3.14.1–9, 24–25, Grihapati’s birth and naming
review: Read birth and naming; assembled guests are narrative witnesses, not relatives inferred from attendance.

reference: Shiva Purana 3.15.50–58, Grihapati receives Agni’s office; Agnishvara
review: Read 50–58: disguise, appointment and named cult site. Do not transfer this incarnation’s parents to independently attested Agni records.

reference: Shiva Purana 3.24.1–5, 41–63, Pippalada’s family and manifestation
review: Read the birth and family verses. Fig-tree nurturing is distinct from biological ancestry; Bhṛgu family membership is not a specified immediate parent.

reference: Shiva Purana 3.25.2–21, Pippalada, Padma and their children
review: Read marriage, ten unnamed sons and protection from Saturn. Narrative coercion is retained; unnamed children receive no invented identities.

reference: Metropolitan Museum of Art, object 2000.42.4, Panel fragment with the god Shiva/Oesho, curatorial description
review: Read object description and metadata. Museum iconographic identification remains distinct from linguistic interpretation; no relatives inferred from a worshipper or proposed family shrine.

reference: Jeff Watt, Himalayan Art Resources, Mahakala introduction: identity, functions and source traditions
review: Read identity, emanation and functions; names denote a category, not one universal family.

reference: Jeff Watt, Himalayan Art Resources, Six-armed Mahakala: traditions and iconographic differences
review: Read one-face/six-arm form and transmission; other six-arm traditions have different origins.

reference: Jeff Watt, Himalayan Art Resources, White six-armed Mahakala: Shangpa tradition
review: Read wealth function and emanation. Teacher lineage is not genealogy; unnamed iconographic consort not guessed.

reference: Jeff Watt, Himalayan Art Resources, Lha Chenpo: Nyingma and Mindrolling contexts
review: Read identification and Nyingma/Mindrolling context; no Hindu household imported.

reference: Jeff Watt, Himalayan Art Resources, 75 Forms of Mahakala (Erroneous Belief), 2020
review: Read terminology correction and retinue classification. Seventy-five lords are not seventy-five manifestations.

reference: Shiva Purana 3.17.1–18, ten named forms and their Shaktis
review: Read the full chapter. These names designate explicitly described forms. Tārā is not automatically the registered wife of Bṛhaspati; Mahākāla is not automatically a Tibetan or Bai genealogy. The repeated Śakti reading is a textual issue, not permission to invent a partner.

reference: W. J. Wilkins, Hindu Mythology, Vedic and Puranic (1900), pp.335–341, Karttikeya: separate birth traditions
review: Read separate birth narratives and marriage. Kept Agni/Ganga, Agni/Svaha and the existing Shiva Purana account selectable rather than aggregating parents. No automatic Prajapati→Brahma resolution.

reference: A Short Illustrated Kanda Puranam, Murugan Bhakti, prior lives and concluding marriage paragraphs
review: Read prior-life and marriage paragraphs. Named biological father differs from unnamed adoptive father; Indra’s daughter reserved to owner. Narrative opponents and army members are not inferred family.

reference: Thomas Stamford Raffles, The History of Java (1830), vol.I pp.428–429: incarnations and pedigree
review: Read pp.428–429. Registered named intermediates and incarnation-specific parents. Rahwana receives a separate conflicting pedigree; Indian names are not automatically selected as targets. The following Wiwaha synopsis is a separate narrative context.
